segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Six days later Jesus took with him Peter, James, and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain by themselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he was transformed in front of them: his face shone like the sun, and his clothes became white as the light.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And suddenly Moses and Elijah appeared to them, talking with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter spoke up and said to Jesus,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you wish, I will put up three shelters here, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While he was still speaking, a bright cloud suddenly overshadowed them, and a voice came from the cloud, saying,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “This is my Son, the beloved, with whom I am well pleased. Listen to him!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces and were terrified.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus came and touched them and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Get up, and do not be afraid.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when they looked up, they saw no one but Jesus himself, alone.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Tell no one about the vision until the Son of Man has been raised from the dead.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The disciples asked him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Elijah does come, and he will restore everything.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they wanted. In the same way the Son of Man too is about to suffer at their hands.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the disciples understood that he had spoken to them about John the Baptist.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they came to the crowd, a man approached him, knelt before him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, have mercy on my son, for he has seizures and suffers terribly; he often falls into the fire, and often into the water.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I brought him to your disciples, and they could not heal him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you? How long am I to put up with you? Bring him here to me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus rebuked the demon, and it came out of him, and the boy was healed from that very hour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the disciples came to Jesus privately and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why could we not drive it out?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Because of your little faith. For truly I tell you, if you have faith like a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move, and nothing will be impossible for you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they were gathering in Galilee, Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The Son of Man is about to be handed over into human hands,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and they will kill him, and on the third day he will be raised.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they were deeply grieved.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they came to Capernaum, the collectors of the two-drachma tax approached Peter and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Your teacher pays the two-drachma tax, doesn’t he?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Yes.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when he came into the house, Jesus spoke to him first:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth collect tolls or poll tax, from their own sons or from others?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “From others,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Then the sons are free.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But so that we do not give them offense, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up. When you open its mouth you will find a four-drachma coin; take that and give it to them for me and for you.”

notes.note: The traditional 'transfigured' comes from the Latin Bible and survives in English almost only for this event. The Greek verb is an ordinary word for a change of form or appearance, and the same verb is usually rendered 'transformed' in Romans 12:2 and 2 Corinthians 3:18. 'Transformed' gives the plain sense a first-century reader would have heard.

The word means a tent or temporary hut. It is the Septuagint's term both for the wilderness tabernacle and for the booths of the Feast of Booths, and many interpreters hear an echo of that festival in Peter's offer. Some manuscripts read 'let us make' rather than 'I will make'.

The voice repeats the words spoken at Jesus's baptism (Matthew 3:17) and adds a command. Most interpreters hear an echo of Deuteronomy 18:15, where Moses promises a prophet like himself and says, 'you shall listen to him'. With Moses and Elijah present, the command singles out Jesus as the one to be heeded.

The expectation rests on Malachi 4:5–6, where God promises to send the prophet Elijah before the day of the Lord to restore the hearts of fathers and children. Jesus's reply in verse 11 uses the same verb, 'restore', that the Greek version of Malachi uses.

The Greek verb is literally 'is moonstruck', reflecting the ancient belief that recurring seizures were tied to the phases of the moon. The symptoms described fit what is now called epilepsy, and many modern versions say 'epileptic'. 'Has seizures' describes the condition without importing either the ancient theory or a modern diagnosis; verse 18 attributes the boy's condition to a demon.

The word describes something bent out of shape and so morally distorted. 'Perverse' is the usual rendering, but in current English it tends to suggest either mere contrariness or sexual deviance. The phrase echoes Deuteronomy 32:5 in the Greek version, where Moses calls Israel a 'crooked and twisted generation'.

The Greek says only 'Jesus rebuked him/it, and the demon came out of him'. The pronoun could refer to the boy or to the demon. Most translations take it as the demon, since 'rebuke' is the usual verb for Jesus's commands to unclean spirits, and the translation makes that explicit.

notes.phrase: nothing will be impossible for you
notes.note: Verse 21 of the traditional numbering ('But this kind does not come out except by prayer and fasting') is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is not printed in the Greek text translated here. It is generally thought to have been added by copyists from the parallel in Mark 9:29. Some manuscripts also read 'unbelief' rather than 'little faith' earlier in this verse.

The Greek plays on a single word: the 'Son of Man' (literally 'son of the human being') is to be handed over into the hands of 'human beings'. The word refers to people in general rather than males, and 'human hands' keeps something of the echo. The verb 'handed over' is the same one elsewhere rendered 'betrayed' or 'delivered'.

This was the annual contribution of two drachmas, equal to a half-shekel, paid by adult Jewish men for the upkeep of the Jerusalem temple, on the basis of Exodus 30:13. It was not a Roman tax. This explains Jesus's argument in verses 25–26: the tax is owed to God, and a king's sons do not pay their father's tax.

The 'sons' may be the king's own family, as opposed to everyone else, or the king's own people, as opposed to subject foreigners. Most interpreters take it as the royal family, which fits the application: Jesus, and by extension his disciples, stand to God as sons, not as taxpayers. 'Sons' is kept so that the link with 'my Son' in verse 5 remains audible.

notes.traditional: a piece of money (KJV); a shekel
notes.note: The Greek names a specific coin, the stater, worth four drachmas. That is exactly the two-drachma tax for two people, which is why it covers both Jesus and Peter.

candidates.reason: 'Scribe' now suggests a copyist rather than an expert in the Jewish law, so the choice between 'scribes', 'scholars of the law' and 'teachers of the law' should be made once for all the Gospels and Acts.
It is frequent across the Gospels and Paul and is variously rendered 'offend', 'cause to stumble' and 'cause to sin'; the senses need a governed set of renderings.
The choice between 'hand over', 'betray' and 'deliver' recurs throughout the passion predictions and narratives and affects how Judas's act and God's are read.
It is rendered 'transfigured' in Matthew and Mark but 'transformed' in Romans 12:2 and 2 Corinthians 3:18; one decision would let readers see that it is the same verb.
Jesus's formula 'amen I say to you' occurs dozens of times across the four Gospels and is rendered 'truly', 'verily', 'amen' or 'I assure you'; it must be uniform.
